{{short description|Polynomial with only one term}}
In [[mathematics]], a '''monomial''' is, roughly speaking, a [[polynomial]] which has only one [[summand|term]]. Two definitions of a monomial may be encountered:

# A monomial, also called a '''power product''' or '''primitive monomial''',<ref name=":0">{{Cite book |last=Lang |first=Serge |title=Algebra |publisher=Springer Verlag |year=2005 |edition=Revised 3rd |series=GTM 211 |location=New York |pages=101}}</ref> is a product of powers of [[Variable (mathematics)|variables]] with [[nonnegative integer]] exponents, or, in other words, a product of variables, possibly with repetitions. <ref name="Dummit 2004 238">{{Cite book |last1=Dummit |first1=David S. |title=Abstract Algebra |last2=Foote |first2=Richard M. |publisher=John Wiley and Sons |year=2004 |isbn=978-0-471-43334-7 |edition=3rd |location=Hoboken, NJ, USA |pages=297}}</ref> For example,<math>x^2yz^3=xxyzzz</math> is a monomial. The constant <math>1</math> is a primitive monomial, being equal to the [[empty product]] and to <math>x^0</math> any variable <math>x</math>. If only a single variable <math>x</math> is considered, this means that a monomial is either <math>1</math> or a power <math>x^n</math> of <math>x</math>, with <math>n</math> a positive integer. If several variables are considered, say, <math>x, y, z,</math> then each can be given an exponent so that any monomial is of the form <math>x^a y^b z^c</math> with <math>a,b,c</math> non-negative integers (taking note that any exponent <math>0</math> makes the corresponding factor equal to <math>1</math>).

# A monomial in the first sense is multiplied by a nonzero constant, called the '''[[coefficient]]''' of the monomial. <ref name=":0" /> A primitive monomial is a special case of a monomial in this second sense, where the coefficient is <math>1</math>. For example, in this interpretation, <math>-7x^5</math> and <math>(3-4i)x^4yz^{13}</math> are monomials (in the second example, the variables are <math>x, y, z,</math> and the coefficient is a [[complex number]]).

In the context of [[Laurent polynomial]]s and [[Laurent series]], the exponents of a monomial may be negative, and in the context of [[Puiseux series]], the exponents may be [[rational number]]s.

In [[mathematical analysis]], it is common to consider polynomials written in terms of a shifted variable <math>\bar{x}  = x - c</math> for some constant <math>c</math> rather than a variable <math>x</math> alone, as in the study of [[Taylor series]].<ref name=":9">{{Cite book |last1=Saff |first1=E. B. |title=Fundamentals of Complex Analysis |last2=Snider |first2=Arthur D. |publisher=Pearson Education |year=2003 |isbn=0-13-907874-6 |edition=3rd |pages=242}}</ref><ref name=":2">{{Cite book |last=Apostol |first=Tom M. |title=Calculus |publisher=John Wiley & Sons |year=1967 |isbn=0-471-00005-1 |edition=2nd |volume=1 |location=USA |pages=274–277, 434}}</ref> By a slight [[abuse of notation]], monomials of shifted variables, for instance <math>2\bar{x}^3  = 2(x - c)^3,</math> may be called monomials in the sense of '''shifted monomials''' or '''centered monomials''', where <math>c</math> is the '''center''' or <math>-c</math> is the '''shift'''.

Since the word "monomial", as well as the word "polynomial", comes from the late Latin word "binomium" (binomial), by changing the [[prefix]] "bi-" (two in Latin), a monomial should theoretically be called a "mononomial". "Monomial" is a [[syncope (phonetics)|syncope]] by [[haplology]] of "mononomial".<ref>''American Heritage Dictionary of the English Language'', 1969.</ref>

== Comparison of the two definitions ==
With either definition, the set of monomials is a subset of all polynomials that is closed under multiplication.

Both uses of this notion can be found, and in many cases the distinction is simply ignored, see for instance examples for the first<ref>{{cite book | last = Cox | first = David |author-link=David A. Cox |first2=John|last2=Little |author-link2=John B. Little (mathematician) |first3=Donal|last3=O'Shea |author-link3=Donal O'Shea | title = Using Algebraic Geometry | publisher = Springer Verlag | year = 1998 | pages = [https://archive.org/details/springer_10.1007-978-1-4757-6911-1/page/n2 1] | url =https://archive.org/details/springer_10.1007-978-1-4757-6911-1| isbn = 0-387-98487-9 }}</ref> and second<ref>{{Springer|id=M/m064760|title=Monomial}}</ref> meaning. In informal discussions the distinction is seldom important, and tendency is towards the broader second meaning. When studying the structure of polynomials however, one often definitely needs a notion with the first meaning. This is for instance the case when considering a [[monomial basis]] of a [[polynomial ring]], or a [[monomial order]]ing of that basis. An argument in favor of the first meaning is that no obvious other notion is available to designate these values,{{citation needed|date=October 2024}} though primitive monomial is in use and does make the absence of constants clear.<ref name=":0" />

''The remainder of this article assumes the first meaning of "monomial".''

==Monomial basis==
{{main|Monomial basis}}
The most obvious fact about monomials (first meaning) is that any polynomial is a [[linear combination]] of them<ref>{{Cite web |title=Polynomial is Linear Combination of Monomials - ProofWiki |url=https://proofwiki.org/wiki/Polynomial_is_Linear_Combination_of_Monomials |access-date=2026-01-18 |website=proofwiki.org}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Monomials and polynomials |url=https://www.mathplanet.com/education/algebra-1/factoring-and-polynomials/monomials-and-polynomials |access-date=2026-02-24 |website=Mathplanet |language=en}}</ref>, so they form a [[basis (linear algebra)|basis]] of the [[vector space]] of all polynomials, called the ''monomial basis'' - a fact of constant implicit use in mathematics.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Interpolation in the monomial basis |url=https://drlvk.github.io/nm/section-monomial-basis.html |access-date=2026-02-24 |website=drlvk.github.io}}</ref>

==Number==
The number of monomials of degree <math>d</math> in <math>n</math> variables is the number of [[multicombination]]s of <math>d</math> elements chosen among the <math>n</math> variables (a variable can be chosen more than once, but order does not matter), which is given by the [[multiset coefficient]] <math display="inline">\left(!!\binom{n}{d}!!\right)</math>. This expression can also be given in the form of a [[binomial coefficient]], as a [[polynomial expression]] in <math>d</math>, or using a [[Pochhammer symbol#Alternate notations|rising factorial power]] of <math>d+1</math>:
<math display="block">\left(!!\binom{n}{d}!!\right)
= \binom{n+d-1}{d} = \binom{d+(n-1)}{n-1}
= \frac{(d+1)\times(d+2)\times\cdots\times(d+n-1)}{1\times2\times\cdots\times(n-1)}
= \frac{1}{(n-1)!}(d+1)^{\overline{n-1}}.</math>
The latter forms are particularly useful when one fixes the number of variables and lets the degree vary. From these expressions one sees that for fixed ''n'', the number of monomials of degree ''d'' is a polynomial expression in <math>d</math> of degree <math>n-1</math> with leading coefficient <math display="inline">\frac{1}{(n-1)!}</math>.

For example, the number of monomials in three variables (<math>n=3</math>) of degree ''d'' is <math display="inline">\frac{1}{2}(d+1)^{\overline2} = \frac{1}{2}(d+1)(d+2)</math>; these numbers form the sequence 1, 3, 6, 10, 15, ... of [[triangular number]]s.

The [[Hilbert series]] is a compact way to express the number of monomials of a given degree: the number of monomials of degree <math>d</math> in <math>n</math> variables is the coefficient of degree <math>d</math> of the [[formal power series]] expansion of
<math display="block"> \frac{1}{(1-t)^n}.</math>

The number of monomials of degree at most {{math|''d''}} in {{math|''n''}} variables is <math display="inline">\binom{n+d}{n} = \binom{n+d}{d}</math>. This follows from the one-to-one correspondence between the monomials of degree <math>d</math> in <math>n+1</math> variables and the monomials of degree at most <math>d</math> in <math>n</math> variables, which consists in substituting by 1 the extra variable.

==Multi-index notation==

The ''[[multi-index notation]]'' is often useful for having a compact notation, specially when there are more than two or three variables. If the variables being used form an indexed family like <math>x_1, x_2, x_3, \ldots,</math> one can set
<math display="block">x=(x_1, x_2, x_3, \ldots),</math>
and
<math display="block">\alpha = (a, b, c,\ldots).</math>
Then the monomial
<math display="block">x_1^a x_2^b x_3^c \cdots</math>
can be compactly written as
<math display="block">x^{\alpha}.</math>

With this notation, the product of two monomials is simply expressed by using the addition of exponent vectors:
<math display="block">x^\alpha x^\beta=x^{\alpha+\beta}.</math>

==Degree<!-- [[Degree of a monomial]] redirects here -->==
{{Unreferenced section|date=November 2025}}
The degree of a monomial is defined as the sum of all the exponents of the variables, including the implicit exponents of 1 for the variables which appear without exponent; e.g., in the example of the previous section, the degree is <math>a+b+c</math>. The degree of <math>x y z^2</math> is 1+1+2=4. The degree of a nonzero constant is 0. For example, the degree of −7 is 0.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Marecek |first=Lynn |last2=Anthony-Smith |first2=MaryAnne |last3=Mathis |first3=Andrea Honeycutt |date=2020-04-22 |title=6.1 Add and Subtract Polynomials - Elementary Algebra 2e {{!}} OpenStax |url=https://openstax.org/books/elementary-algebra-2e/pages/6-1-add-and-subtract-polynomials |access-date=2026-07-26 |website=openstax.org |language=English}}</ref><ref name="CoxLittleOShea2015">{{cite book |last1=Cox |first1=David A. |last2=Little |first2=John |last3=O'Shea |first3=Donal |title=Ideals, Varieties, and Algorithms: An Introduction to Computational Algebraic Geometry and Commutative Algebra |edition=4th |publisher=Springer |year=2015 |isbn=978-3-319-16720-6}}</ref>

The degree of a monomial is sometimes called order, mainly in the context of series. It is also called total degree when it is needed to distinguish it from the degree in one of the variables.<ref name="CoxLittleOShea2015" />

Monomial degree is fundamental to the theory of univariate and multivariate polynomials. Explicitly, it is used to define the [[degree of a polynomial]] and the notion of [[homogeneous polynomial]], as well as for graded [[monomial ordering]]s used in formulating and computing [[Gröbner basis|Gröbner bases]]. Implicitly, it is used in grouping the terms of a [[Taylor series#Taylor series in several variables|Taylor series in several variables]].<ref name="CoxLittleOShea2015" /><ref name="MillerSturmfels2005">{{cite book |last1=Miller |first1=Ezra |last2=Sturmfels |first2=Bernd |title=Combinatorial Commutative Algebra |publisher=Springer |year=2005 |isbn=978-0-387-22356-2}}</ref>

==Geometry==
{{Unreferenced section|date=November 2025}}
In [[algebraic geometry]] the varieties defined by monomial equations <math>x^{\alpha} = 0</math> for some set of α have special properties of homogeneity. This can be phrased in the language of [[algebraic group]]s, in terms of the existence of a [[Group action (mathematics)|group action]] of an [[algebraic torus]] (equivalently by a multiplicative group of [[diagonal matrix|diagonal matrices]]). This area is studied under the name of ''[[Toric geometry|torus embedding]]s''.<ref name="MillerSturmfels2005" /><ref name="CoxLittleSchenck2011">{{cite book |last1=Cox |first1=David A. |last2=Little |first2=John B. |last3=Schenck |first3=Henry K. |title=Toric Varieties |publisher=[[American Mathematical Society]] |year=2011 |isbn=978-0-8218-4819-7}}</ref>
